During our membership in the Security Council in 2023 and 2024, Ecuador stated that the dire situation for the people in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea and the systematic violations of their human rights contrasted with the diversion of enormous resources towards illicit nuclear weapon and ballistic missile programs. A definitive, peaceful, diplomatic, and political solution to the situation in the Korean Peninsula is urgently needed. We must also reverse the growing trend among children who are suffering from undernourishment and malnourishment, and we must ensure that they have access to education and health care services. Ecuador would encourage pursuit of the three key pillars of the United Nations: peace and security, human rights, and development. This is essential to build fairer, more peaceful and stable societies. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

I thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this crucial meeting and all the briefers for their insightful remarks. I deeply appreciate Ms. Kim and Ms. Kang for bravely sharing their personal and heartbreaking experiences. A decade after the Commission of Inquiry highlighted human rights violations in the DPRK, Japan is deeply concerned grave violations continue and the situation has deteriorated even further, as today's speakers have emphasized. During Japan's most recent term on the Security Council, the discussions in June last year and August 2023 on the situation in the DPRK underscores its human rights violations are also inexplicably linked with the building up of its military capabilities, including the pursuit of unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs. Essential resources are being diverted for this purpose at the expense of people's welfare, despite their significant unmet needs. Furthermore, the disregard continues by engaging in unlawful military cooperation with Russia, including through sending its soldiers to fight against Ukraine, which constitutes a clear violation of international law, including the UN Charter. and in the procurement of its weapons and ammunition. Japan strongly urges Pyongyang to take tangible measures to address serious human rights violations, cease its unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programs, halt its military cooperation with Moscow, and fully comply with all relevant Security Council resolutions and return to dialogue. Mr. President, I must also draw attention to a grave human rights violation, the abductions of Japanese citizens, including Ms. Yokota Megumi, who was abducted by North Korea, by North Korea agents in Niigata 47 years ago, then just 13 years old. The act of international abductions infringes on a nation's sovereignty and jeopardizes the well-being and safety of its students. The abductions issue has been unresolved for decades. The abductees have remained trapped for almost half a century, while the abductees and their families have advanced in age. Most recently, Mr. Arimoto Akihiro passed away in February at the age of 96. without being able to reunite with his daughter who was abducted by North Korea during her study in Europe in 1983. Megumi's 89-year-old mother, Yokota Sakie, has become the only living parent of the 12 abductees who are identified by the government of Japan and still have not returned to Japan. In addition, There are many other cases in which the possibility of abduction cannot be ruled out. Literally speaking, there is no time left. Japan's plight is shared by others. The COI report acknowledges individuals from Republic of Korea, China, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Lebanon, Malaysia, Romania, Singapore, and Thailand have also endured this hardship. Japan strongly urges Pyongyang to immediately return all abductees and asks for international community to unite in concerted effort to secure their return. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Our statement is aligned with the statement made by the representative from the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defense of the Charter of the United Nations. Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, It is an honor for me to take the floor on behalf of the Government of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea at this high-level plenary meeting in the General Assembly. We welcome this opportunity to speak in a debate which is as sensitive as this one is, namely the issue of human rights in the DPRK. Let me begin by reiterating the firm commitment of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea to the provisions of the UN Charter, the principles of which are sovereignty among states, sovereign equality, non-interference in internal affairs, and mutual respect. These must all be observed in all international deliberations. And yet, we note with concern the growing use of human rights as a political instrument by some international actors. These campaigns are selective in nature. They're politicized, they use double standards, and they run counter to the universal and balanced principle of human rights. They lead to mistrust, confrontation, and a dangerous breakdown in the multilateral system. The Universal Declaration on Human Rights and international norms were designed to guarantee dignity for all human beings, but today we are seeing through the use of the argument that efforts are being made in self-defense, that these fundamental human principles of international law are being violated. And this is a direct threat to stability and peace among nations. The issue of human rights arises in one way or another in almost all countries, and the human rights system of a state must be assessed from the standpoint of cooperation and dialogue and not simply by imposing unilateral condemnation. Equatorial Guinea believes that any review process must be bear in mind the voice of the affected people and the particular context of each country and absolute respect for their sovereignty. Constant interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states disguised as humanitarian concern infringes upon the dignity of nations and it distorts the legitimate mechanisms of human rights. Excellencies, in an increasingly polarized world, we must work for an international order based on equity, respect, and solidarity, promoting genuine human rights must not divide people, but rather unite them. In view of this, the government of my country stands with the people of the DPRK in defense of their sovereignty, dignity, and the principle of noninterference, which must prevail among nations. And at the same time, we call for the issue of human rights in this country to be addressed in accordance with the tenets of the United Nations Charter. Thank you very much, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Mr. President, China consistently opposes the forced discussion of country-specific human rights issues without considering our country concerned, and opposes selective, politicized, and double-standard approaches to human rights. Despite DPRK's strong position, certain countries have in a selective manner forcibly pushed for GA's discussion of DPRK's human rights situation, escalating the abuse of the UN platform and turning human rights issues into a political tool to pressure the country. Such acts gravely violate the sovereignty of member states, worsen confrontation in human rights domain, and hurt the credibility of the UN in human rights work. While certain countries cry out for more attention from UN to DPRK's human rights situation, they are unrelenting in the unilateral coercive measures against the country. The UN human rights experts have repeatedly pointed out that such UCMs severely affect the people's rights to health and an adequate standard of living in DPRK. These measures are among the biggest obstacles to achieving national development goals, and their humanitarian and livelihood negative impacts cannot be ignored. This fully demonstrates that these countries care about is by no means the human rights or people's well-being in the DPRK. For these countries, the issue of human rights is nothing but a political tool to attack, smear, and pressure the DPRK. Once again, China strongly urges these countries to immediately lift the UCMs that are in violation of international law and the basic norms of international relations and stop exploiting human rights issues to interfere in other countries' internal affairs. Finally, like to point out that with regard to the individuals who enter China illegally for economic reasons, China has consistently handled these cases based on a principled position that combines domestic law, international law, and humanitarian considerations. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus.

Mr. President, the Republic of Belarus has consistently favoured effective cooperation in the area of human rights based on the principles of universality, impartiality and objectiveness. To our great regret, we have to note that today's meeting is underpinned by completely different ideas. it by bias, by disdain and selectivity. We express disappointment in the ongoing trend to mix up the noble ideas of fighting for human rights with a de facto fighting against individual states using various excuses. It's clear that the decades-long sanctions inter alia through the use of illegal unilateral coercive measures imposed upon the Democratic People's Republic of Korea using human rights excuses de facto is against the rights of its citizens. We believe that the international community needs to admit that the lack of results and harm of these measures is significant and change the way that they interact with the DPRK. We need to move from accusing, depriving, and restricting to having respectful and depoliticized dialogue. We are convinced that only this way can we really expand and protect human rights. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belarus. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Peru.

Thank you, President. I would like to thank the presidency of the General Assembly and responsible delegations of this organization for this meeting, which enables us to reflect about a specific situation where hundreds of thousands of people do not have the necessary assurances that they can exercise their fundamental freedoms and the most basic human rights. At the same time, this is a timely meeting because in today's world, many people seem to have forgotten the importance of protecting dignity and well-being for all peoples to ensure international peace and security. And states are the ones who have the primary responsibility for promoting and protecting human rights. The United Nations human rights architecture was built on the basis of states' duty to cooperate. Latin America has lived through many periods with unfathomable challenges. with regard to fundamental rights. And in fact, the first special procedures of the then UN Commission on Human Rights, both country-specific mandates and thematic mandates, were established to address specific situations happening in our region. Latin American history over the past 40 or 50 years has taught us that these special procedures should be understood not so much as a hurdle for governments, but rather as a valuable tool to contribute to the protection of human rights. At the same time, the current circumstances in our hemisphere and in other regions of the world present us with serious and many human rights challenges. Then, as now, the universal system mechanisms are key tools to contribute to addressing those challenges and ensuring reparations for victims. And that is why Peru has supported the efforts of our organization in reaffirming human rights anywhere in the world. My delegation knows firsthand the irreproachable credentials of the Human Rights Special Rapporteur, Salmon, in the GPRK, and we welcome the impartial way in which she is carrying out her mandate. Similarly, Peru agrees with the perspective Ms. Salmon has used in her reports. She takes a victim-centered approach to human rights violations. In this context, my delegation would call on all parties involved with the material mandate for this meeting to cooperate actively in the work being carried out by the Special Rapporteur. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Peru. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, the Russian Federation has consistently failed to support the practice of adopting selective unilateral resolutions on human rights in individual countries. We believe this method of work to be ineffective. It does not enable the protection and expansion of human rights and only serves to heighten confrontation between states. Such resolutions are being promoted by a group of Western countries for political purposes. The real situation with human rights in the DPRK, and in any other country, is of no interest to them. For example, European countries look on indifferently and sometimes are even complicit in the deaths of thousands of migrants in the Mediterranean, and they are indifferent to bans on language use in a number of EU countries and their allies. or indifferent to persecution and bans on churches and congregations, Islamophobia, or the glorification of Nazism. However, these situations, for some reason, are not brought by Western countries for consideration by the UNGA. Today's meeting is a stark example of the ineffective use of the UN's resources during this financial crisis, since this meeting essentially is duplicatory and it tries to replace the Universal Periodic Review procedure. This works well as part of the UN Human Rights Council. This procedure, unlike today's meeting, is applicable to all, and it is fully in line with a key principle of the sovereignty equality of states. It provides an opportunity for constructive and mutually respectful dialogue in the human rights area. The DPRK, in November last year, successfully completed this procedure. All states and civil society had an opportunity to present their comments, proposals and reports. The DPRK, in turn, reported on the adoption of an amendment to dozens of laws and legislative acts in the area of human rights. This has led to improvements in its legal system and has helped to improve people's well-being and ensure the effective enjoyment of human rights. It should be pointed out that despite its limited resources, the DPRK coped well with the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, it managed to overcome the aftermath of the devastating floods in the northwestern districts as a result of the torrential rains in July last year. Children were able to return to school on time. The DPRK supports free elementary, middle, and higher education. At the state level, there are measures to provide students and school pupils with everything they need free of charge. There are free school and children's meals. The DPRK has dealt with homelessness in Tallinn by building large-scale housing complexes both in the capital and in the provinces, thanks to developing agriculture using technology, the DPRK has made headway in improving its food security. The efforts of the DPRK in improving and protecting human rights are bearing fruit despite significant external challenges. There is increasing impetus to the West's stance to stifle Pyongyang's economy and to whip up the military threat and besmirch the country's leadership into a lie by introducing politicized and non-objective the resolutions of the UNGA. Along these lines, there is a lack of desire to review the parameters of the UN Security Council sanctions regime. This has long lost its relevance and no longer helps to address the issues facing the Korean Peninsula. Pyongyang also has an unprecedented unilateral sanctions regime against it, and many of these sanctions affect ordinary people. The UN Security Council's Sanctions Committee barely makes basic requests regarding the provision of humanitarian assistance. We are firmly against this, which significantly prevents obstacles for the sovereignty, development, and protection of human rights in the DPRK. We can witness that, as the DPRK stated in its UPR report, It will continue to strengthen and improve its legal system in the area of human rights and will conscientiously comply with its commitments under international conventions to which it is a state party, such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the CEDAW Convention as well. As regards some accusations that I've heard from a number of delegations in this hall regarding the cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. We have laid out our position. The DPRK is our close neighbor and partner. We are developing relations in every area with it. This is our sovereign right. Russia cooperates cooperation with the DPRK is in line with international law, and Moscow and Pyongyang are acting fully in line with international law, in particular the Chapter 4 of 2024 agreement. This provides for swift assistance if there is an attack on another party, and we are always going to be grateful to Pyongyang and to the DPRK for their assistance. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland.

Mr. President, Switzerland would like to thank you for convening this high-level meeting on the human rights situation in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. We'd also like to thank the Assistant Secretary General for Human Rights and also the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the DPRK for their briefings. We particularly welcome the testimonies of the representatives from civil society. Switzerland remains concerned by serious and systematic violations of human rights and possible crimes against humanity committed in the DPRK. The list of these violations is long: arbitrary detention, torture, forced disappearance to political prisoner camps, strict control of the media, and the promulgation of laws that severely limit the freedom to research, receive, and disseminate information. and also deprivation of food, healthcare, access to water, and sanitation services. We would like to recall the DPRK's obligations to immediately bring an end to all these violations and to uphold its international obligations. We also underscore the DPRK's commitment and obligation, rather, to protect human rights of its men and women citizens. who've been repatriated and we urge all states to respect the principle of non-refoulement. The population of the DPRK has the right to live enjoying justice and dignity. The establishment of accountability is crucial to ensure that the rule of law be respected and to guarantee. the rights of victims. This requires criminal prosecution, reparation and also non-judicial measures such as the quest for the truth and institutional reforms. Everything needs to place victims at the heart of these processes. We would urge the DPRK to conduct investigations on these crimes in order to bring an end to impunity. For Switzerland, which for more than seven decades now has worked for peace on the Korean Peninsula, in particular as part of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission and also as the chair of the 1718 Security Council Sanctions Committee over the past two years, For Switzerland, the respect for human rights and the maintenance of peace in the region is, and beyond, these things are closely linked. Switzerland would like to reiterate that the use of UN mechanisms in the area of human rights is crucial. Here, a lack of access to the country and to reliable data makes any up-to-date evaluation of the human rights situation in the DPRK extremely difficult. This is extremely worrisome, that there is such an opaque situation. Switzerland would the DPRK to provide a standing invitation to all special rapporteurs and to authorize unhindered access to its country for international organizations. Switzerland would also encourage the DPRK to accept a large amount of the recommendations of the UPR of November 2024 and to ensure that these recommendations be implemented rapidly and effectively. Thank you very much indeed.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Luxembourg.

Mr. President, Luxembourg joins itself with the statement made by the European Union and would like to make the following comments in its national capacity. We welcome the decision of the President of the General Assembly to convene this high-level meeting on human rights in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. thus following up the request made by the Assembly in resolution 79/181 of December 2024. We would also like to thank all the participants of this open session, in particular those who have shared their lived experiences. Their courage and bravery is admirable, and through their testimonies, we are really able to grasp how very serious the situation is. We would urge the international community to continue to heed their voices and more systematically involve them in the decision-making processes which affect them. The most recent commission of inquiry of the UN on the DPRK in 2014 noted systemic, generalized, and serious violations of human rights. slavery, torture, political, religious, racial persecution, persecution based on sexual belonging, and forced disappearance. Sexual violence and gender-based violence is also prevalent and used as a tool of repression by the state. It is therefore crucial to include gender indicators in the early warning systems and the evaluations of the risk of atrocities. 11 years later, the situation has hardly changed. Perhaps it's even become more international, with the active implication or involvement of North Korea in the war of aggression conducted by Russia against Ukraine. We condemn this in the strongest possible terms. Sir, we welcome the fact that the Human Rights Council mandated in 2024 the updating of the Commission of Inquiry's report, and we're very much looking forward to the outcome of this work. As a member of the Council last year, we're particularly proud of having supported this resolution. It is high time to act. We would call upon all stakeholders, including members of the Security Council, to take our responsibilities as members of the international community very seriously and protect people from crimes against humanity and also to ensure that each and every person can enjoy his or her inherent inalienable rights. Thank you very much.
Distinguished representative of Luxembourg. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Panama.

Mr. President, Panama believes that human rights are the underpinning of any society's aspirations, and we reaffirm our firm commitment to the UN Charter, which establishes fundamental rights and freedoms for all human beings. We strongly believe that these guarantees are universal, indivisible, and interdependent, and that Respecting them lays the foundation for peace, security, and sustainable development. In this context, we recognize the valuable work done in the Human Rights Council and by the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the DPRK. We are particularly concerned at persistent reports of human rights violations as documented by independent UN mechanisms, including the Human Rights Commission of Inquiry in the DPRK. The use of forced labor by the DPRK raises a wide range of serious human rights concerns. In particular, we are concerned with the institutionalization of this practice by using their own people as a means for producing and manufacturing war material. That matter deserves greater scrutiny by the international community. We call for a constant constructive stance aimed at peace, including compliance with Security Council resolutions to ensure regional stability and denuclearization in the Korean Peninsula. We believe that the path to a lasting solution in the Korean Peninsula requires not just respect for international law, but also a commitment to the well-being and the dignity of all North Korean citizens. We support all diplomatic efforts aimed at denuclearization, regional stability, and a tangible improvement in the human rights situation in the DPRK. Similarly, Panama joins in the call for a return for UN agency staff and other humanitarian agency staff to the DPRK so that they can address the urgent needs of the most vulnerable people. We reiterate that all States are obligated to promote and protect human rights and fundamental freedoms, as well as to comply with the obligations they have shouldered pursuant to various international instruments. We also call for continued work to promote human rights worldwide through dialogue and joint efforts. we renew our determination to work together to ensure that the United Nations remains a strong and effective platform and a credible platform for addressing global challenges. This is an opportunity to send a clear message that the international community will not tolerate human rights violations and that the UN will continue to work to avoid threats to international peace and security, always guided by our collective desire to have a safer world for everyone. Panama reaffirms its commitment to the principle that international security must be a collective responsibility, and it must be pursued decisively by all members of the international community. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Panama. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Czechia.

Mr President, Czechia fully aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, and now I'd like to add a few words in my national capacity. Following the adoption of General Assembly resolution 79/181, we have this important opportunity to gather here in the presence of human rights defenders, civil society representatives, and escapees from the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to demonstrate our firm commitment to and support for the people of the DPRK. The critical findings of the 2014 Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights Violations and Abuses remain largely unaddressed. It is essential to reiterate that the government of the DPRK must tackle these long-standing issues decisively and comprehensively. The High Commissioner's long-awaited report, which will provide an update on the human rights situation in the DPRK and assess the implementation of the Commission's recommendations due in spring 2027, will be crucial for our further deliberations. Human rights are universal and intrinsic to every human being, a principle recognized by all UN member states. We remain deeply concerned about the systematic, widespread and grave human rights violations, and equally by the pervasive culture of impunity and lack of accountability that prevails in the DPRK. In this regard, we strongly urge the DPRK Government to promptly implement the recommendations made during the fourth cycle of its Universal Periodic Review. Fundamental freedoms, notably freedom of expression and freedom of movement, remain severely curtailed. We therefore urge the DPRK authorities to repeal all repressive policies and fully recognize the fundamental right of their citizens to freely leave and return to their own country. The refoulement of escapees to the DPRK is unacceptable. Returnees face torture, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment, as well as other serious human rights violations, as confirmed by the findings of the Commission and subsequent investigations by the Office of the High Commissioner. The DPRK government must also cease putting vital resources into weapons and missile programs that breach the relevant UN Security Council resolutions to the detriment of the well-being of its people. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Czechia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Israel.

Honorable President, Israel thanks the President of the General Assembly for convening this important meeting in accordance with resolution 79/181 to address the ongoing human rights violations in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. We are deeply alarmed by the persistent reports of systematic abuse, torture, extrajudicial executions, widespread sexual and gender-based violence, and the state's total control over every aspect of its citizens' lives. These are not isolated incidents. They are part of a deliberate and institutionalized policy of repression. President, the DPRK's internal oppression does not remain within its borders. It is directly linked to the regime's relentless pursuit of weapons of mass destruction and the military expansion of the country. A government that silences its people, that rules through fear and violence, is the same government that diverts scarce resources to develop nuclear warheads, ballistic missiles, and other weapons. Some proliferate to the Middle East and other regions. This model, the fusion of domestic brutality with global aggression, is tragically mirrored by another regime, Iran. The Iranian regime also brutalizes its own people while pursuing a military nuclear program and spreading terror across the region. Both regimes exploit their populations to invest in weapons of mass destruction, and both defy the international community with impunity. This is not a theoretical threat. On October 7th, Israel experienced the deadliest attack on its civilians in decades. Among the weapons used by Hamas terrorists during the massacre were North Korean manufactured arms. This disturbing fact demonstrates how DPRK proliferation fuels terrorism across the globe. The same weapons built through the suffering of the North Korean people were used to murder and terrorize innocent civilians in Israel. We cannot separate human rights from global security. Where regimes repress their own people, they often export violence beyond their borders. The DPRK's partnership with other malign actors, including Iran and terrorist proxies, must not be overlooked. The international community must remain united in its call for accountability. We support the full implementation of Security Council Resolutions 1718 and 2397, and we reiterate the need for a complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Israel. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nicaragua.

Mr. President, the UN General Assembly is the most representative body. As the main place for multilateral deliberations, it promotes the fundamental principles enshrined in the UN Charter, such as sovereign equality among states, noninterference in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. In recent years, we have noted a growing manipulation by some Western countries who exploit this body to impose their political agendas against specific countries, violating the principles of the UN Charter. Under the pretext of defending human rights or democracy, Western countries promote biased resolutions and selective condemnation. They ignore realities and they undermine non-interference in internal affairs, which is a fundamental principle for international law. This practice weakens multilateralism and turns the General Assembly into an instrument for political pressure. This is counterproductive in the peaceful settlement of disputes. Clear examples are resolutions submitted against certain States, such as today's resolutions, while They ignore flagrant human rights violations committed by Western countries, particularly against national minorities and migrants. This double standard erodes the credibility of the UN and furthers geopolitical divisions rather than promoting constructive dialogue. Mr. President, Nicaragua recalls that these plenary meetings reflect the particular political interests, and they lack objectivity and impartiality. We must respect the sovereign decisions of states when it comes to mechanisms and models for ensuring human rights in accordance with their national specificities. Nicaragua continues to denounce politicization, double standards, and the manipulation of human rights to justify any type of measures or acts of aggression against sovereign states. Mr. President, we reaffirm our commitment to the promotion and protection of all human rights on an equal footing with mutual respect, and we reiterate our firm opposition to their use for political purposes. We call for full respect for sovereignty, self-determination, territorial integrity, and non-interference in internal affairs of the DPRK. Mutual respect, solidarity, and bolstered multilateralism are essential for the genuine spirit of the General Assembly, a forum where all nations, without coercion or manipulation, can debate on an equal footing. The international community must reject these unilateral and discriminatory actions, which violate the UN Charter and only exacerbate global tensions. Genuine respect for inclusive multilateralism and sovereignty of peoples will guarantee international peace and stability. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nicaragua. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine.

President, Ukraine thanks Assistant Secretary-General Eliza Brans-Gerris, Special Rapporteur Elizabeth Salmon, and all debriefers for their substantive presentations and impactful firsthand testimonies. Ukraine also aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, and we would like to make the following remarks in our national capacity. We remain deeply concerned about the dire human rights situation in the DPRK. For decades, there has been no meaningful progress, nor any constructive engagement by the DPRK with the international community or relevant UN mandates. Beyond the severe domestic repression of its own people, the Pyongyang regime has expanded its destabilizing role internationally by openly supporting Russia's war of aggression against my country, Ukraine, a war marked by some of the gravest violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. This support includes the transfer of weapons to the Russian Federation, which are used to destroy civilian infrastructure and kill civilians, including women, children, persons with disabilities, and the elderly. According to open-source data, the DPRK currently supplies approximately 50% of Russia's ammunition needs, including 4 million artillery shells, multiple launch rocket systems, and short-range ballistic missiles. All this in clear violation of UN Security Council resolutions. Furthermore, in the autumn of 2024, North Korea reportedly deployed a military contingent to support Russia, estimated at 10,000 till 12,000 soldiers. We commend the Special Rapporteur for addressing these critical issues in her latest report to the Human Rights Council, which reflects the gravity of this development. North Korean soldiers have been used by Russia as a cannon fodder. According to some testimonies from captured soldiers, their leadership kept them in the dark, not telling that they are being deployed to fight against Ukrainians. According to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, DPRK military losses in Russia's war have reached nearly 5,000 killed and wounded. Of the three North Korean brigades deployed, one has been completely eliminated. while the other two have suffered significant casualties. The recent public acknowledgement by dictators Putin and Kim Jong-in of DPRK troop participation in Russia's war effort marks the emergence of a dangerous axis of evil. This alliance not only contributes to the further escalation of aggression, but also poses a broader threat to international peace and security. Instead of aiding foreign wars, The DPRK should redirect its resources to address the critical needs of its own people, who continue to suffer under an oppressive regime. We call on the DPRK to immediately cease its support for Russia's war crimes in Ukraine and to fully comply with its obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law. We also urge the international community to hold the DPRK accountable for its actions, both at home and abroad. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ukraine. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Albania.

Mr. President, I thank you for convening this critical discussion and express our gratitude to Ms. Ilse Brint Skarries, Assistant Secretary General for Human Rights, and Ms. Elizabeth Salmon, Special Rapporteur about human rights in the Democratic Republic of Korea for their insightful briefings. Their analysis highlights the inseparable link between the human rights crisis in North Korea and the pursuit of peace and stability in the Korean Peninsula and beyond. Ms. Kim, Ms. Kang, your personal stories and tireless work echo my own country's history under dictatorship, reminding us of the human cost of repression. Mr. Skahot and Mr. Chong, your organization's efforts give voice to millions silenced by the DPRK regime. Your courage and advocacy move us profoundly. You all together compel this Assembly to act. Distinguished delegates and colleagues, this discussion here in the General Assembly is a vital step to confront a situation that has deteriorated further. Over 25 million North Koreans live under a regime that perpetrates systematic, widespread, and gross human rights violations. Mr. President, we remain deeply concerned regarding the human rights situation in DPRK. In recent years, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea has enacted several laws that included death penalty provisions further restricting the enjoyment of the right of freedom of movement, to work, and to freedom to expression and opinion, among other rights. Surveillance has tightened, political prison camps have expanded, independent media, civil society, and religious freedom remain banned, while collective punishment, torture, and forced labor crush any opposition. Children face malnutrition, and women and girls endure trafficking and sexual violence in detention. Mr. President, given the severity and complexity of the human rights situation in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, accountability measures should be ensured as everyone has the right to remedy when their human rights are violated, in line with international norms and standards. Investigation and prosecution of serious crimes are indispensable, as are measures to ensure the right of victims and societies to know the truth about violations, the right of victims to reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence of violations. In this context, we must strengthen accountability mechanisms, support Ms. Salomon's mandate, and amplify survivor voices to hold the regime accountable. Mr. President, The DPRK obsession with militarization, diverting resources to unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programs in defiance of Security Council resolutions, starves its people of food, medicine, and hope. These violations fuel regional instability and mock the UN Charter. As members of this Assembly, we are bound by international law to place human rights at the core of multilateralism. Adopting a human rights-based and comprehensive approach to accountability, placing the rights and needs of victims at the center of the design and implementation of accountability processes in DPRK is crucial. Albania remains committed to work jointly with all Member States to support a future where North Koreans can enjoy freedom and human rights. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Albania. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Maldives.

Thank you, President.

I thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this high-level plenary meeting. I also thank the presenters for their valuable insights and perspectives. Each and every country has the obligations which it must fulfill for its people. The modern rule-based order requires each member state of the United Nations to adhere to a framework of rules, norms, and institutions that guarantees the rights of all persons. the multilateral system rests on the responsibilities of states and the trust between states. The Democratic People's Republic of Korea, as a member state of the United Nations, must be held accountable for the abuse and violation of these obligations and rights. The report of the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in DPRK is concerning. Systematic human rights violations and abuse and limitation cooperation within the United Nations strengthens against the entities a decade after commission of inquiries remains disheartening fact the tight control and restriction exerted over its population and the imposition of severe penalties perpetrators a culture of intimidation and fear Each sovereign and independent state has the right to its own government, but the government has the fundamental obligation to serve the interest of its people, not an act in the interest of a select few. The DPRK's declaration last year to pivot away from reunification and towards aggression, militarization strains the trust and cooperation built over the past eight decades. Modern geopolitics cannot afford to regress the strides we have painstakingly achieved. What is needed is dialogue, demilitarization and diplomacy. The Maldives recognize the efforts by the DPRK in engaging with the United Nations and its mechanisms, including the Human Rights Council. The Maldives urges the Government of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to immediately and urgently heed the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry, Special Rapporteur, and the international human rights mechanism.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Maldives. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Colombia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to international human rights instruments. In current circumstances, where conflicts are taking place at a global level, multilateralism seems to be under threat, and there is a persistent need to defend multilateralism for humanity. Colombia firmly supports the work of verification mechanisms in the area of human rights, including extending the mandate of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as of the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the DPRK. Mr. President, Colombia notes with concern the persistent human rights violations in this country, which have been pointed to by a number of UN fora, forced labor, child labor, that have been reported on by the Special Rapporteur in July of 2024. Colombia also expresses its concern at the apparent worsening of the situation when it comes to guaranteeing human rights in that country. According to the recent report at the last Human Rights Council session, there has been increased restriction to information and the freedom of expression, and the unacceptable generalized use of the death sentence have been reported on by staff of the office. The DPRK seemed to accept the recommendations with regard to health, food, and education, but it did not accept the recommendations on political prisoner camps, nor the commitment the comment of the Special Rapporteur on forced labor and other activities. The work of the Special Rapporteur has shown that the obligations in accordance with international law are not being complied with. They must protect the freedom of expression, the right to life and adequate food, and the state policies seem not to be complying with these obligations. Colombia takes advantage of this opportunity to call upon States not to fail to defend human rights internationally. We must continue to seek to improve conditions so that we leave no one behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Colombia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Lao People's Democratic Republic.

Mr. President, the Lao PDR reaffirms its long-standing position that issues relating to human rights should be addressed through constructive, non-confrontational, non-politicized dialogue and based on mutual respect and principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. It is our firm belief that all human rights mechanisms must carry out their mandates in impartial, objective, and non-selective manner, while respecting the authoritative information provided by the concerned state. Avoiding politicization and double standards is essential in fostering trust and cooperation. which are prerequisites for tangible progress. We continue to support efforts to promote genuine dialogue and cooperation between states and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. We encourage all stakeholders, including relevant UN human rights mechanisms, to provide technical assistance based on the request and consent of the state concerned in support of national efforts to strengthen institutional capacity and improve the promotion and protection of human rights. In this regard, the Lao PDR encourages the international community and all concerned parties to pursue practical avenues for constructive and meaningful dialogues with the DPRK in view of enhanced mutual understanding and cooperation in the area of human rights. Mr. President, in conclusion, my delegation reaffirms its commitment to fulfilling its international human rights obligations and to enhance cooperation with the United Nations.

And ASEAN human rights mechanisms.

We remain guided by the principles of the impartiality, transparency, objectivity, non-politicization, and constructive engagement, taking into account the diverse national circumstances and priorities of all countries in our shared effort to advance the cause of human rights. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Lao People's Democratic Republic. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkey.

Thank you, Mr. President. Upholding human rights remains a cornerstone of international peace, security, and dignity, and Turkey attached high priority to protection and promotion of these international universal values. Turkey remains deeply concerned by the ongoing human rights violations in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, as documented in numerous UN reports. We have constantly supported the international efforts to address this issue and co-sponsored key resolution adopted by the Human Rights Council as well as by the General Assembly's Third Committee. These resolutions reflect the serious and shared concern of the international community, reaffirm the imperative of ensuring accountability for those responsible for such violations. Turkey supports mandates of the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea and the Office of the High Commissioner for the Human Rights Field Office in Seoul. We call on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to cooperate fully with United Nations mechanism and to fulfill its international human rights obligations. We also encourage the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to adopt a cooperative approach in addressing different issues regarding its relations with the international community, such as allowing the return of UN agencies and facilitating them to carry out their mandates. Mr. President, beyond the human rights situation, we remain deeply concerned by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's continued development of weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs in violation of multiple UN Security Council resolutions. We urge the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to comply fully with its international obligations and to refrain from any actions that could further heighten the tensions in the region. The promotion of human rights and complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula must remain at the core of our collective approach to establishing lasting peace and stability in the region. Turkey reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, as well as to the objectives of the Treaty on NPT. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Turkey. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of New Zealand.

The President, New Zealand is alarmed at the appalling state of human rights in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. It is critical that the international community voices our collective concern in a coordinated and sustained manner. Over 10 years since the publication of the report of the Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in the DPRK, We remain gravely concerned by the DPRK regime's lack of action and the ongoing deterioration of the human rights situation. We also remain deeply concerned about reports of executions, abductions, arbitrary detention, torture, and sexual violence. We join others in condemning the failure of the DPRK authorities to hold accountable those responsible for these grave human rights abuses that, in many cases, the Commission of Inquiry also found constitute crimes against humanity.

New Zealand is committed to the abolition of the death penalty worldwide.

We are particularly concerned by the DPRK's Law on Rejecting Reactionary Thought and Culture, which contains grossly disproportionate punishments, including the death penalty, for accessing information and foreign content. We urge the DPRK regime to immediately halt all public executions and abolish the death penalty in all cases. We are distressed by the prevalence of malnutrition, severe hunger, and widespread health problems in the DPRK. In particular, we are seriously concerned about the impact on the most vulnerable, including children, women, and persons with disabilities. We condemn the DPRK regime's continuing diversion of the country's scarce resources towards its development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles at the expense of the well-being of its people. We reiterate calls for the DPRK regime to allow the return of the United Nations Development Programme and other international humanitarian agencies to support the basic needs of North Koreans.

We continue to urge the DPRK to engage with the recommendations of its November 2024 Universal Periodic Review. We hope that through meaningful cooperation with UN human rights mechanisms, the DPRK will engage in crucial reforms to better protect and promote the rights of its people.

Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of New Zealand. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. President. Germany aligns itself with the EU statement. We are deeply concerned by the systematic, widespread, and gross human rights violations of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Despite repeated calls from the international community, the human rights situation remains one of the worst in the world, affecting millions of innocent individuals. We welcome that the General Assembly considers the situation of human rights in the DPRK. When a UN Member State so flagrantly violates its international commitments, we need to act. We owe it to the United Nations. We owe it to the people of North Korea. More than 10 years After the Commission of Inquiry released its report on arbitrary detention, forced labor, executions, torture, and restrictions on freedom of expression, movement, and association, these human rights violations are still being committed. They are well documented by UN human rights mechanisms and civil society. We are particularly concerned by the enforced disappearances, the forced repatriations of North Korean escapees, as well as the inhumane treatment, including torture and forced labor. We welcome the report to the Human Rights Council from February 2025 by UN Special Rapporteur Elizabeth Salmon. In the report, she underscored how basic rights, such as access to adequate food, health, education, and water and sanitation, are persistently denied while the supply of necessities and the delivery of humanitarian assistance to the people of North Korea remain limited. The principle of universality of human rights is a cornerstone of international human rights law, underscoring the belief that all humans deserve fundamental rights and freedoms simply by virtue of being human. Sovereignty cannot and should not be used as a shield to justify the violation of human rights. And while the DPRK uses sovereignty as a convenient justification to undermine the human rights of its own people, it also blatantly violates the sovereignty of another UN Member State through its expanded military cooperation with Russia and the ongoing transfer of material and troops in support of Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. Germany continues to support the mandate of the UN Special Rapporteur, and we urge the DPRK to grant her access to the country to engage further with UN mechanisms and to implement the recommendations of its November 2024 Universal Periodic Review and the Human Rights Council. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Argentina.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Argentina is deeply concerned at the reports on the human rights situation in the DPRK. Available reports describe systematic violations of human rights, including kidnappings, forced disappearances, arbitrary executions, torture, starvation, and other very serious violations against the right to life, which is essential for all other rights. We are particularly concerned about allegations of violations against the rights of women and the rights of children through practices such as forced abortion and infanticide, according to the most recent report of the UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the DPRK, Ms. Elizabeth Salmon. In addition to these violations, there are severe restrictions on fundamental freedoms, such as the freedom of thought, expression, and religion. These forms of repression, which undermine the human spirit, are equally intolerable, and they are a serious affront to human dignity. For these reasons, Argentina once again co-sponsored the annual resolution on this issue in the Human Rights Council in Geneva. And at the same time, we co-sponsored the joint declaration on the human rights situation in the DPRK. as well as the stakeout before accredited press at the UN in the margins of the briefing on 12 June 2024. Finally, Mr. President, Argentina believes that it is the responsibility of all Member States of the international community to continue to work to put an urgent end to the serious violations on the right to life and human dignity in the DPRK. We must exhaust all possible channels and explore new ways of achieving this common goal. As established in Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood. It is this brotherly duty which leads us to redouble our efforts to find a solution to this scourge. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina. We have heard the last speaker in the plenary segment. And with your thanks to the secretariat and the interpreters for their flexibility, the high-level plenary meeting to address the human rights abuses and violations being committed in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is now concluded. The meeting is adjourned.
